scenes.text: Last year, Costco sold almost two hundred and seventy billion dollars' worth of stuff. And here's the strange part. The stuff is not really where the profit comes from.

Costco collected five point three billion dollars in membership fees. Its entire net profit for the year? About eight point one billion. So a plastic card in your wallet is worth roughly two thirds of everything Costco keeps.
By the end of this video, you'll understand the machine behind that number, and you'll know the exact math that tells you whether a Costco membership is actually worth it for you.

scenes.chapter: Two ways to run a store
scenes.text: Most stores play a simple game. Buy a product, mark it up, sell it, keep the difference. Costco plays a different game. It wants to make as little as possible on the product, and then charge you for the right to walk in the door.

On the left, a normal retailer: profit from every item on the shelf. On the right, Costco: products sold near cost, and profit from the membership. That one flip changes everything. The prices, the store layout, even the hot dogs. Let's go piece by piece.

In fiscal twenty twenty-five, membership fee income rose ten percent, from four point eight to five point three billion dollars. Part of that came from a fee increase in September twenty twenty-four. The basic Gold Star membership went from sixty to sixty-five dollars, and Executive went from one hundred twenty to one hundred thirty.

Now think about what a membership actually costs Costco to deliver. The warehouse is already built. The staff are already paid. The lights are already on. So when you pay sixty-five dollars, almost all of it drops straight toward profit. It's the closest thing in retail to free money.

elements.text: What does a membership cost Costco to deliver?

scenes.text: And people keep paying. In the U.S. and Canada, ninety-two point three percent of members renew. Worldwide, it's about ninety percent. Plenty of streaming services would celebrate keeping customers that well, and they don't ask you to drive to a warehouse.

And the machine is huge. At the end of fiscal twenty twenty-five, Costco had eighty-one million paid members, one hundred forty-five million cardholders, and nine hundred fourteen warehouses around the world.
But why would anyone pay just to go shopping? The answer is the most disciplined pricing rule in retail.

elements.text: → the strictest pricing rule in retail

scenes.text: Costco has long been reported to cap its markups. Around fourteen percent on branded goods, and fifteen on its own Kirkland Signature products. A typical supermarket can mark items up far more than that.

This isn't generosity. It's strategy. If prices are reliably low, the membership feels like it pays for itself. If the membership pays for itself, you renew. And renewals are the profit. So Costco will happily make almost nothing on a television, because the TV is just the reason you keep the card.
Walk into a typical supermarket and you'll find tens of thousands of different products. Costco carries roughly four thousand. That sounds like a weakness. It's actually a weapon.

When Costco orders a product, it orders it in enormous volume, for more than nine hundred warehouses at once. That gives it huge bargaining power with suppliers. Fewer products also means faster moving inventory, simpler stores, and less waste.
And when a supplier won't hit Costco's price? Costco just makes the product itself.

Kirkland Signature is Costco's private label, and one of the biggest consumer brands in the world by sales. Store brands give a retailer two things: a better margin than name brands, and leverage. If a big brand demands a higher price, Costco can put its own version right next to it. Kirkland is also a loyalty engine. You can't buy most of it anywhere else. Want Kirkland? You need the card.
And then there's the famous hot dog and soda combo. A dollar fifty. The same price since nineteen eighty-five. Adjusted for inflation, that price should be several times higher today.

Costco keeps it at a dollar fifty anyway, because the hot dog isn't a product. It's a promise. It tells every member: we will not squeeze you. And that promise is worth far more than the margin on a hot dog.

That attitude starts at the very top. Former Costco CEO Craig Jelinek has said that when he once suggested raising the hot dog price, co-founder Jim Sinegal told him, more or less: if you raise the hot dog, I will kill you. The price never moved.

elements.text: — co-founder Jim Sinegal (as retold by Craig Jelinek)

scenes.text: There's one more quiet trick: the bulk pack. When everything comes in a giant pack, every trip becomes a big trip. You spend more per visit, the membership feels worth it faster, and you have less reason to shop anywhere else in between.

scenes.chapter: Is a membership worth it for you?
scenes.text: So is a basic membership worth it for you? Here's the honest math. Gold Star costs sixty-five dollars. If buying at Costco saves you ten percent compared with your usual store, you need to spend six hundred fifty dollars a year, about fifty-four dollars a month, just to break even. If it only saves you five percent, that bar doubles to thirteen hundred. So before you join, look at what you actually buy, not what you might buy.

elements.text: buy what you actually use — not what you might

scenes.chapter: The Executive tier: is it worth it?
scenes.text: Now here's the part most people miss. Costco has two kinds of members. The Executive tier costs one hundred thirty dollars a year, and pays you two percent back on eligible purchases, up to one thousand two hundred fifty dollars a year. Executive members are just under half of all paid members, but they account for nearly three quarters of Costco's sales.

So is Executive worth it for you? The upgrade costs sixty-five dollars more than Gold Star. Sixty-five divided by two percent is three thousand two hundred fifty. If you spend more than about three thousand two hundred fifty dollars a year at Costco, roughly two hundred seventy a month, the upgrade pays for itself. Spend less, and it doesn't.

elements.text: spend over $3,250 a year (≈ $270 a month)  →  YES

scenes.text: So: low prices, a cheap hot dog, a small product range, and a tier that pays you back. How does all that add up to eight billion dollars of profit? Let's put the machine together.

elements.text: low prices  •  $1.50 hot dog  •  ~4,000 products  •  2% back

scenes.text: Step one: low prices attract members. Step two: more members means more buying power. Step three: more buying power means even lower prices from suppliers. Step four: lower prices make the membership more valuable, so people renew, and new members join. Every turn of that wheel adds more fee income at the center. It's a loop that feeds itself. And the bigger Costco gets, the harder it is for anyone to copy.

On paper, any retailer could do this. In reality, it's brutal. To run on razor-thin margins, you need massive scale from day one. You need members who trust you before you've earned it. And your shareholders have to accept that you'll deliberately leave money on the table on every sale. Most companies simply can't stomach that. Costco has done it for decades, which is exactly why its customers believe the prices.

The model isn't invincible. If renewal rates slip, the most profitable piece of the business shrinks fast. Fee increases have to be rare. Raise them too often, and the feeling that it pays for itself breaks. And online shopping makes the warehouse trip less special every year. But for now, the numbers say the machine is running stronger than ever.

elements.text: for now: running stronger than ever

scenes.text: So, how does Costco make money? It sells you groceries at almost no profit, so that you'll happily pay it every year for the privilege of buying them. The store is the bait. The membership is the business.

elements.text: groceries at ≈ $0 profit  →  you pay every year to shop

scenes.text: And the lesson goes far beyond Costco. When customers pay you before they buy anything, you can afford to make every purchase feel like a win. That's why gyms, streaming apps, and software companies all chase subscriptions.

elements.text: get paid first  →  make every purchase feel like a win

scenes.text: And Costco isn't the only company hiding its real business. Airlines, for example, make billions not from flying, but from credit cards. That breakdown is next. Subscribe so the machine keeps running, and I'll see you in the next one.
